title: What really happens when you injure your shoulder
summary: NH explains that shoulder injuries are almost always structural (rotator cuff or AC joint), not muscle tears, citing a non-English study where only 2 of 400 injured lifters had a muscle (front-delt) tear, both from kipping pull-ups. Shoulder vulnerability comes from rotation limiting safe range of motion, as with behind-the-neck pressing.

claims.claim: Shoulder injuries are very common in bodybuilding, powerlifting and athletics because the shoulder's range of motion is limited and its rotation changes the range you can safely go through.
Behind-the-neck pressing is bad for the shoulder while a deep front overhead press isn't, because the shoulder girdle's rotation behind the head can't sustain the deep range of motion.
'Shoulder injury' almost always means a structural injury, not a muscle injury.
A non-English study he read found only 2 of 400 lifters with shoulder injuries had muscle tears (always the front delt); the rest were structural injuries to the rotator cuff or AC joint.
The three delt heads are very resilient; when something gives during presses or push-ups, it is the rotator cuff or AC joint beneath.
The two front-delt tears in the study came from kipping pull-ups, so don't kip.
The structural shoulder injuries came from flaring elbows while pressing, overuse from too much horizontal pressing, or behind-the-neck pressing.
